title: Level 12: SPI Master — Driving a MAX7219 LED Matrix
aim: To configure the ATmega328P as an SPI master and communicate with a MAX7219 LED matrix driver over the SPI bus, sending register-address and data byte pairs to display patterns.
objective: Understand the SPI bus topology (MOSI, MISO, SCK, SS), master mode register configuration (SPCR, SPSR), the SPI data exchange mechanism, chip-select framing, and the MAX7219's register-based command protocol.
theory:
SPI — Serial Peripheral Interface

SPI is a synchronous, full-duplex, master-slave serial protocol developed by Motorola. Unlike UART, it uses a shared clock line (SCK) generated by the master, enabling higher speeds (up to 10+ MHz). A 4-wire SPI bus uses:

  • MOSI (Master Out Slave In) — master sends data to slave
  • MISO (Master In Slave Out) — slave returns data to master (simultaneously)
  • SCK (Serial Clock) — master-generated clock synchronises all transfers
  • SS/CS (Slave Select / Chip Select) — pulled LOW by master to address a specific slave

SPI is synchronous (shared clock) and full-duplex (sends and receives simultaneously in one transfer). It has no built-in addressing — SS lines identify each slave.

SPI Clock Modes (CPOL/CPHA)

SPI has 4 operating modes defined by CPOL (Clock Polarity) and CPHA (Clock Phase):

ModeCPOLCPHAClock idleSample on
000LOWRising edge
101LOWFalling edge
210HIGHFalling edge
311HIGHRising edge

The MAX7219 uses SPI Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0).

ATmega328P SPI Pins

  • PB5 (SCK) = Arduino Pin 13
  • PB4 (MISO) = Arduino Pin 12
  • PB3 (MOSI) = Arduino Pin 11
  • PB2 (SS) = Arduino Pin 10 (software-controlled for the MAX7219 CS)

SPCR — SPI Control Register

  • SPE (bit 6) — SPI Enable
  • MSTR (bit 4) — Master mode (1) vs Slave mode (0)
  • CPOL (bit 3), CPHA (bit 2) — Clock mode
  • SPR1:SPR0 (bits 1:0) — Clock prescaler with SPI2X in SPSR: 00 = ÷4 (4 MHz at 16 MHz)

SPSR — SPI Status Register

  • SPIF (bit 7) — SPI Interrupt Flag. Set when transfer completes. Clear by reading SPSR then SPDR.
  • SPI2X (bit 0) — Double speed bit. With SPI2X=1, actual SCK = F_CPU/(2×prescaler).

SPI Transfer Mechanism

Writing a byte to SPDR (SPI Data Register) initiates a transfer. MOSI shifts out MSB first; MISO shifts in simultaneously. When all 8 bits complete, SPIF is set. The received byte is in SPDR. Polling: while(!(SPSR & (1<<SPIF)));.

MAX7219 Protocol

Each MAX7219 command is a 16-bit word: 8-bit register address + 8-bit data. The master asserts CS LOW, sends the 16 bits (two SPI transfers), then deasserts CS HIGH. The MAX7219 has registers for each digit (0x01–0x08), plus control registers: DECODE_MODE (0x09), INTENSITY (0x0A), SCAN_LIMIT (0x0B), SHUTDOWN (0x0C), and DISPLAY_TEST (0x0F).

pretest.question: What are the four SPI bus signals?
pretest.explanation: SPI uses MOSI (Master→Slave data), MISO (Slave→Master data), SCK (master clock), and SS/CS (chip select, active-LOW).

pretest.question: How does SPI differ from UART?
options: SPI uses a shared master-generated clock (synchronous); UART is clockless (asynchronous)
pretest.explanation: SPI's shared SCK clock synchronises data sampling, enabling higher speeds (MHz range). UART requires no clock wire but both sides must independently generate matching baud rates.

pretest.question: What does CPOL=0, CPHA=0 (SPI Mode 0) mean?
options: Clock idle HIGH, sample on falling
Clock idle LOW, capture on rising edge
Clock idle HIGH, capture on rising
Clock idle LOW, capture on falling
pretest.explanation: Mode 0: CPOL=0 = clock idle LOW, CPHA=0 = data sampled on the leading (rising) edge. This is the most common SPI mode used by most sensors and displays.

pretest.question: Which ATmega328P pin is MOSI?
pretest.explanation: MOSI is on PB3 (Arduino Uno Pin 11). PB4=MISO, PB5=SCK, PB2=SS (hardware SS pin).

pretest.question: Which bit in SPCR enables Master mode?
pretest.explanation: MSTR (Master/Slave Select, bit 4 of SPCR) sets the SPI module as master (1) or slave (0). Must be 1 along with SPE to operate as SPI master.

pretest.question: How do you initiate an SPI transfer?
pretest.explanation: Writing a byte to SPDR (SPI Data Register) starts the transfer. The SPI hardware automatically shifts out the byte on MOSI while simultaneously shifting in a byte on MISO.

pretest.question: When is the SPIF flag set in SPSR?
options: When all 8 bits of a transfer have completed
pretest.explanation: SPIF (SPI Interrupt Flag) is set in SPSR after all 8 bits have been shifted. Poll it to know when the transfer is complete before reading or writing SPDR again.

pretest.question: What is the SPI clock frequency with SPR1=0, SPR0=0, SPI2X=0 at 16 MHz?
pretest.explanation: SPR1=0, SPR0=0, SPI2X=0 gives SCK = F_CPU/4 = 16 MHz/4 = 4 MHz. The MAX7219 supports up to 10 MHz SCK.

pretest.question: How big is each MAX7219 command?
pretest.explanation: Each MAX7219 command is 16 bits: an 8-bit register address followed by 8-bit data. Sent as two consecutive SPI bytes with CS held LOW throughout.

pretest.question: Why must CS be held LOW for the entire 16-bit MAX7219 transfer?
options: MAX7219 latches 16 bits into its command register only on the CS rising edge (LOAD pin)
pretest.explanation: The MAX7219 treats the rising edge of its LOAD/CS pin as the latch signal. If CS goes HIGH between the two bytes, only the first byte is latched — an incomplete command.

procedure: Include #include <avr/io.h>. Define SS pin: #define CS_PIN PB2. Wire: Arduino Pin 11 (MOSI) → MAX7219 DIN, Pin 13 (SCK) → CLK, Pin 10 (CS) → LOAD. Power MAX7219 from 5V with 10 µF and 100 nF decoupling capacitors on VCC.

Configure SPI pins: MOSI (PB3), SCK (PB5), and CS (PB2) as outputs. MISO (PB4) stays as input (hardware configured by SPE): DDRB |= (1<<PB3)|(1<<PB5)|(1<<PB2);. Set CS HIGH initially: PORTB |= (1<<CS_PIN);.
Configure SPCR: enable SPI (SPE=1), set master mode (MSTR=1), SPI Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0 — both 0 by default), prescaler ÷16 (SPR1=0, SPR0=1) → 1 MHz SCK: SPCR = (1<<SPE)|(1<<MSTR)|(1<<SPR0);.

Write the SPI transfer function: pull CS LOW, write address byte, poll SPIF, write data byte, poll SPIF, set CS HIGH: void max7219_write(uint8_t addr, uint8_t data) { PORTB &= ~(1<<CS_PIN); SPDR=addr; while(!(SPSR&(1<<SPIF))); SPDR=data; while(!(SPSR&(1<<SPIF))); PORTB |= (1<<CS_PIN); }

Initialize the MAX7219 registers: set SHUTDOWN mode off (0x0C, 0x01), DECODE_MODE none (0x09, 0x00) for raw segment control, SCAN_LIMIT all 8 digits (0x0B, 0x07), INTENSITY medium (0x0A, 0x08), DISPLAY_TEST off (0x0F, 0x00).
Write patterns to digit registers 1–8 (addresses 0x01–0x08). Each digit register accepts an 8-bit pattern where each bit controls one LED column. For a checkerboard pattern, alternate 0xAA and 0x55.

In the main loop, create a scrolling or animation effect by cycling patterns across the digit registers with a short delay. The MAX7219 handles multiplexing of all 64 LEDs internally — you only need to update 8 registers.

Optionally chain multiple MAX7219 modules in series (daisy-chain): cascade DOUT of one to DIN of next. Send N×16 bits of data before releasing CS HIGH — each MAX7219 shifts its data to the next module.

posttest.question: What is the maximum SPI clock frequency the MAX7219 supports?
posttest.explanation: The MAX7219 datasheet specifies a maximum SCK frequency of 10 MHz. The ATmega328P at 16 MHz can achieve 8 MHz (÷2) which is within spec.

posttest.question: SPI is full-duplex. What does this mean?
options: Data is sent and received simultaneously in both directions in a single clock cycle
posttest.explanation: Full-duplex: while MOSI shifts out bits to slave, MISO simultaneously shifts in bits from slave. Every SPI transfer exchanges a byte in both directions.

posttest.question: How would you drive two MAX7219 modules simultaneously?
options: Daisy chain: DOUT→DIN, send 32 bits total, one CS LOW
posttest.explanation: MAX7219 supports daisy-chaining: connect DOUT to next DIN. Keep CS LOW while sending 32 bits (16 per module). The second MAX7219 receives the first 16 bits, the first receives the last 16 bits.

posttest.question: How many LEDs can one MAX7219 drive?
posttest.explanation: The MAX7219 can drive up to 64 LEDs (8×8 matrix) or eight 7-segment displays. It handles multiplexing, current limiting, and brightness control internally.

posttest.question: What does SPI2X bit do?
options: Doubles SPI clock speed for same prescaler setting
posttest.explanation: SPI2X in SPSR doubles the clock frequency. With SPI2X=1 and SPR=00, SCK = F_CPU/2 = 8 MHz (vs 4 MHz without SPI2X).

posttest.question: What is I2C's advantage over SPI in terms of wiring?
options: I2C uses only 2 wires (SCL+SDA) and supports 127 addressable devices with no extra SS lines
posttest.explanation: I2C uses just SCL and SDA for all devices — no per-device SS lines. SPI needs one SS per slave. I2C is lower speed (400 kHz typical) but simpler wiring for many devices.

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: WDT auto-resets MCU when not periodically cleared.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has Port B, C, D only.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile — contents lost instantly on power-off.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: AVR clears I-bit in SREG on ISR entry.

feedback: Brilliant! SPI is the workhorse of high-speed embedded communication — SD cards, LCD displays, ADCs, DACs, and almost every fast peripheral uses SPI. You now understand it at the hardware register level.
